concepts.title: Network Hardware: The Machines That Connect Us
concepts.explanation:
Computers can only share files, printers and software if they are joined together into a network. Think of a network like a group of friends who can all talk to each other. On its own, one computer is like a person standing alone in a room. Connect it to a network and suddenly it can talk to every other device — sharing photos, sending messages, and reaching the whole internet.

There are two ways a device can join a network: with wires, or without wires (wirelessly). Both work well, but each needs different hardware. Hardware means the real, physical machines you could hold in your hand — as opposed to software, which is the programs that run on them. In this part you will meet three key pieces of network hardware.

Connecting with wires: the Ethernet cable

Many devices connect to a network using an Ethernet cable. It looks a little like a thick telephone wire with a clip on the end that clicks into a socket. Wired connections are fast and reliable, but the device cannot move far because it is tied to the cable. Two important devices use these cables to build a network: the switch and the router. They have lots of sockets, so many cables (and therefore many devices) can plug into them at once.

The switch — a meeting point for wired devices

A switch lets you connect wired devices together on one network, such as your school network or an office network. You can plug in many devices, for example:

The switch joins all these devices together so they can communicate — that is, send data to and receive data from each other. Here is the clever part: if you connect a single printer to the switch, then every computer on that network can use that one printer. The switch is like a busy meeting point where all the wired devices come together to talk. On its own, though, a switch cannot reach the internet — it only connects devices that are on the same network.

The router — the doorway to the internet

A router does something different. It lets different networks talk to each other. Its most common job is to connect a small network — like your home or school — to the huge network we call the internet.

For example, a router connects Ehel Academy's network to the internet. Because of the router, any device on the school network can reach the internet — so a student can open a website, watch a lesson video, or send a message to a cousin far away. If you remember only one thing, remember this: it is the router — and only the router — that lets devices on your network reach other networks and the internet.

Connecting without wires: the wireless access point

A wired switch and a wireless access point do a similar job — they both let computers join a network. The big difference is that the wireless access point needs no cables. Devices connect to it through the air. This is perfect for devices that move around, such as:

The most common wireless access point is a Wi-Fi access point. It sends and receives signals — special invisible waves that carry data through the air to and from nearby devices. A huge advantage is that hundreds of devices can connect to a single Wi-Fi access point without any wires at all. Compare that to a wired switch, which needs one separate cable for every single device!

Wi-Fi signals only travel a short distance, though. The further you walk away from the access point, the weaker the signal becomes — until, eventually, your device drops off the network. That is why Wi-Fi access points are often fixed high up on walls or ceilings, sometimes with an aerial sticking out. An aerial is the part that helps send and receive the signals.

How is a wireless access point different from a switch?

If you put a switch and a Wi-Fi access point side by side, the biggest difference is simple: the switch uses cables, while the wireless access point uses signals through the air. A switch is best for devices that stay still, like a desktop computer or a printer. A wireless access point is best for devices you carry around, like a phone or a tablet. Both connect devices to the same network — they just do it in different ways.

Here is how the three devices fit together in a typical network. Read the diagram below from top to bottom — the internet is at the top, and the devices are at the bottom:

A simple network: the router reaches the internet; the switch connects wired devices; the wireless access point connects devices with no wires.

+-----------+ +--------------------+

+-----------+ +--------------------+

In many homes there is just ONE box that plugs into the wall — people call it 'the Wi-Fi' or 'the router'. But that single box is actually doing three jobs at once! Inside it there is a router, a switch, AND a wireless access point, all built together. In a big school or office, these three are often separate machines so they can handle many more devices.

concepts.title: How Data Travels Through Networks
concepts.explanation:
You now know the hardware that joins devices together. But how does a message actually travel from your device, across the world, and arrive at exactly the right computer? That is the amazing journey you will follow in this part.

Cellular networks: the internet almost anywhere

A cellular network is another kind of wireless network, but it works over very large areas. Instead of a small Wi-Fi box on a wall, cellular networks use tall towers (you may have seen them standing high above towns and along roads). These towers send out strong signals that a smartphone can pick up from many kilometres away.

A single cell tower can reach a phone up to about 50 kilometres away, although most of the time the useful range is around 5 kilometres. Making the towers tall is important, because it means the signal is less likely to be blocked by hills or buildings. This is why a mobile phone can connect almost anywhere — from the top of a mountain to the middle of a busy city. Some cars even use cellular networks, so they can download new software or let people make calls from inside the car.

Cellular networks have one big advantage: they cover enormous areas. But they share the same weakness as Wi-Fi — they can suffer from interference. Interference is anything that gets in the way of the signal, such as thick walls or bad weather. When there is interference, the signal may not reach your device properly. This can stop your phone from connecting, or make everything very slow.
concepts.example: Fifty kilometres is a very long way. If you ran around a 400-metre running track, you would have to go around it about 125 times to run 50 km! That is roughly the furthest a single cell tower can send its signal.

concepts.title: Comparing the three ways to connect
concepts.explanation:
You have now met three ways for a device to connect: Wi-Fi, a wired Ethernet cable, and a cellular network (mobile data). Each one suits a different job. You would not want your phone tied to a wire while you walked around a city — and you would not use a slow, faraway cell tower to connect a printer that sits right next to your computer.

One way we compare connections is by their range — how far they reach. Another is their speed. Connection speed is measured in megabits per second, written Mbps. This is the fastest rate at which data can be sent. A higher number means data arrives more quickly, which matters a lot when you are streaming a video or downloading a big file.

IP addresses: every device has its own address

Think of the millions and millions of devices connected to the internet. When your device sends data, how does the internet know which of all those devices to deliver it to? The answer is that every device has its own unique address, called an IP address. IP stands for Internet Protocol.

An IP address is a set of numbers. A common type is made of four numbers separated by full stops, and each number is between 0 and 255. For example, a device might have the address 43.66.141.66. These numbers tell a computer exactly where to send data to, or where to fetch data from. IP addresses are usually created automatically by a small program, so you never have to type them yourself.

The best way to picture an IP address is to think of the address on a letter, or a post code. Every home has its own address so the postal worker knows exactly where to deliver each letter. In the same way, every device has its own IP address so the internet knows exactly where to deliver each piece of data. And just as no two homes on a street can share the same house number, no two devices on a network can share the same IP address — the automatic program makes sure each one is unique, so there is never any confusion.

There are two types of IP address. The older type is called IPv4 — and the world is starting to run OUT of IPv4 addresses, because there are so many devices! So a newer type was invented, called IPv6, which has an almost unlimited number of addresses — enough for every device for a very, very long time.

Here is one of the most surprising ideas about the internet. When you send a message or a photo, it does not travel as one big lump. Instead, before it is sent, the data is chopped up into many small chunks called packets. Packets are usually all about the same size.

Imagine Nadia in Hargeisa wants to send a message to Sami in Mogadishu. Her computer splits the message into, say, three packets. But each packet is not just a piece of the message — it also carries some extra labels. Every packet includes:

the IP address it was sent from (Nadia's device),

the IP address it is going to (Sami's device),

a packet number, so the pieces can be put back in the right order,

and, of course, a small piece of the actual message (the packet data).

Here is what one packet looks like inside. Notice the address labels at the top and the piece of data at the bottom:

One data packet. The 'sent from' and 'sent to' IP addresses are like the return address and destination address on an envelope.

+------------------------------------------+

+------------------------------------------+
concepts.example: Why bother with the return address? Because if a packet gets lost on the way, the computer that was waiting for it knows exactly which device to ask to send it again. The labels make the whole system reliable.

concepts.title: How packets travel and are put back together
concepts.explanation:
When Nadia's packets set off across the internet, something interesting happens: they may take different routes to reach Sami. Just like cars driving from one city to another can take different roads, packets can travel by different paths. Some routes are quicker than others, so the packets often arrive in the wrong order!

This is not a problem, thanks to the packet number. When the packets arrive at their destination, Sami's computer reads the numbers and uses them to put the packets back into the correct order — like sorting shuffled pages of a story back to 1, 2, 3. Only once all the packets have arrived and are in order can the computer read the full message. Here is the whole journey in four steps:

What happens if a packet gets lost?

Sometimes a packet does not arrive at all — it gets lost along the way. When that happens, the internet has a neat way of fixing it:

The receiver computer notices a packet is missing, and sends a message back to the sender asking: "Please send packet 2 again, it got lost."

The sender computer sends another copy of just that one lost packet.

When the copy arrives, the receiver now has all the packets, so it puts them in order.
concepts.example: The full message is complete, and the computer can finally use the data.

concepts.title: Advantages and disadvantages of packets
concepts.explanation:
Splitting data into packets is a clever idea, and it brings real benefits — but it also has a few costs. It is important to understand both sides.

If a packet is lost, only a small piece of data has to be sent again — not the whole message.

Packets do not take up much bandwidth each, so they can travel along a greater variety of connections.
concepts.example: Smaller packets are less likely to get stuck or delayed on a busy network.

concepts.title: How websites are stored and accessed
concepts.explanation:
You use websites every day — but where do they actually live? Every website is stored on a web server. A web server is a powerful computer that keeps all the pages of a website, along with the website's IP address, and it is always connected to the internet so people can reach it at any time.

So what happens when you visit a website? Imagine Sami types the address of Ehel Academy's website into his browser. Here is the journey of his request, step by step:

Sami types a web address into his web browser (a browser is a program such as Firefox). Another name for a web address is a URL — a Uniform Resource Locator. A URL is written as text, for example www.cambridge.org.

His web browser uses the internet to connect to the web server.

Because computers only really understand numbers, the URL is converted into an IP address behind the scenes.

The browser gives the web server that IP address, which tells it exactly where on the server the website is stored.

The web server checks the page is there, then sends the data back to the browser that asked for it — and the page appears on Sami's screen.

This explains a question you might have wondered about: why do we use words in web addresses when computers prefer numbers? The answer is that computers use IP addresses because they only understand numbers, but humans use URLs because words are far easier to remember than a long string of digits. Could you remember the number 93.184.216.34? Probably not — but you could easily remember a name like www.cambridge.org.

"All the packets of my message travel together in a neat line and arrive in order." Actually, no! Packets often split up, take different routes, and arrive jumbled and out of order. That is completely fine — each packet has a number, so the receiving computer sorts them back into the right order before reading the message.

When you visit websites, only use ones that you trust and know are safe. If you are not sure about a website, always check with your teacher, your parents, or a trusted adult BEFORE you visit it. Never type your name, address, school or password into a website you do not know.

concepts.title: Network Failure: When Connections Break
concepts.explanation:
So far, everything has worked perfectly. But networks do not always behave. Cables get unplugged, power goes off, and sometimes whole services stop for hours. In this part you will find out what really happens when a network fails — and why, most of the time, you barely notice.

Let us be very clear about one word. A network is a collection of connections between devices. The internet is simply the biggest network of all — a massive, worldwide web of connections joining computers and devices everywhere. Every day, people all over the world use it for both work and fun. When you connect, you can reach all sorts of services stored on servers, such as:

cloud storage and online banking

holiday bookings and online shopping

messaging services, email and video calls
concepts.example: One of those services is cloud storage. Cloud storage lets you save your files and data on someone else's computer — usually a giant server owned by a big company. These companies have huge servers with enormous amounts of storage space, and they let you use some of it for your own files. The best part is that, because your files are stored on the internet, you can reach them from anywhere in the world — as long as you can connect to the internet. The word 'cloud' does not mean the sky; it just means 'stored on servers somewhere else, reached over the internet'.

concepts.title: Small failures you barely notice
concepts.explanation:
Sometimes the internet seems to fail. What this really means is that one or more of the connections inside it has broken. When a connection breaks, it stops working, and data cannot travel along that route any more.

But here is the wonderful thing. Because the internet is made of so many connections all linked together, the data can simply take a different route to reach its destination. This is why you usually do not even notice when a single connection fails. If one path breaks, the data quietly travels along another one instead:

If one route breaks, data reroutes along the paths that still work.

concepts.explanation:
the server along the RED and YELLOW routes.

Sometimes, though, a large server or a very important connection breaks. Then you might notice that a service you use suddenly stops working, or becomes very slow. Usually there are other servers offering the same service, so your computer can quietly switch to one of those — and things only 'stop working' for a short time.

But if lots of connections fail all at once, it can take many hours, or even days, to fix. Big failures are sometimes caused by a single connection breaking — if that connection is the only path to a server, then the data has no other route to take, and the service goes down completely.

There are many reasons a connection might break, and most of them happen close to home — in the connection between your own device and the internet. For example:

someone accidentally turns off the power;

someone unplugs a cable by mistake;

a fire damages the cables, or stops a server from working.

A helpful way to picture this is to imagine the internet as a set of roads connecting towns and cities. If there are roadworks or an accident on one road, drivers simply choose a different road. That other road might be narrower, so they cannot drive as fast — but they still get where they are going. The internet works in exactly the same way. When a connection breaks, data travels down other routes instead. Those routes get busier, so the data may travel more slowly. That is why, during a failure, you might notice pages take longer to load, or a video keeps stopping and starting.
concepts.example: When something goes wrong, people often shout: "The internet is broken!" But remember: the internet itself does NOT break. It is far too big for that. What actually breaks is just the CONNECTIONS between some of the computers. There are almost always other connections the data can use instead.

concepts.title: The effects of network failures
concepts.example: There is one more danger. Sometimes, during a network failure, data can become corrupted. This means the data is damaged so badly that it cannot be used — and it may be lost forever. That is why saving your work often, and keeping copies, is such a wise habit.

concepts.title: How companies protect against failure
concepts.explanation:
Because large networks — like those of banks, hospitals and big websites — are so important, companies spend a lot of money trying to stop them from failing. Their main trick is to avoid having only one of anything. A large failure is far more likely when there is only a single server, because if it breaks, there is nothing to take over.

So companies make copies of their servers, called backups. If one server breaks, a second, spare server takes over straight away, and users often do not notice anything at all. They also keep backup or 'spare' connections ready, so data always has another route. This idea — having spares ready so the system keeps working even when one part fails — is a hugely important idea in computing. You will use it yourself in your Final Project when you write a plan to keep Ehel Academy's network running.

Some of the biggest network failures in history hit gaming services like the PlayStation Network and Steam. Millions of gamers all around the world suddenly could not play the games they wanted to play — all at the same time! Even the largest companies are not completely safe from network failure.

concepts.title: Staying Safe and Responsible Online
concepts.explanation:
Understanding how networks work also means understanding how to use them safely and kindly. You already value trust, honesty and respect, and you know that other people's privacy matters — and these same values make you a safe and responsible person online. Here is how to put them into practice:

Guard your private information. Never share your full name, home address, school, phone number or passwords with people you do not know online.

Only visit websites you trust. If you are not sure about a site, ask a teacher or a trusted adult before you visit it.

Use a strong password for your accounts, and never share it — not even with a friend. A network with no password lets strangers join, which is why Wi-Fi should always be protected.

Be trustworthy with other people's data. If a friend shares something private with you, keep it private. Do not spread other people's photos or messages without permission.
concepts.example: Think before you type. Be kind and honest in messages. Words sent online can be saved and shared, so write only what you would be happy for anyone to read.

workedExamples.title: Worked example 1: Network Hardware: The Machines That Connect Us
workedExamples.prompt: Which device connects a network to the internet? A) A switch B) A router C) A printer D) An aerial
workedExamples.solution:
Computers can only share files, printers and software if they are joined together into a network. Think of a network like a group of friends who can all talk to each other. On its own, one computer is like a person standing alone in a room. Connect it to a network and suddenly it can talk to every other device — sharing photos, sending messages, and reaching the whole internet.

There are two ways a device can join a network: with wires, or without wires (wirelessly). Both work well, but each needs different hardware. Hardware means the real, physical machines you could hold in your hand — as opposed to software, which is the programs that run on them. In this part you will meet three key pieces of network hardware.

Connecting with wires: the Ethernet cable

Many devices connect to a network using an Ethernet cable. It looks a little like a thick telephone wire with a clip on the end that clicks into a socket. Wired connections are fast and reliable, but the device cannot move far because it is tied to the cable. Two important devices use these cables to build a network: the switch and the router. They have lots of sockets, so many cables (and therefore many devices) can plug into them at once.

The switch — a meeting point for wired devices

A switch lets you connect wired devices together on one network, such as your school network or an office network. You can plug in many devices, for example:

The switch joins all these devices together so they can communicate — that is, send data to and receive data from each other. Here is the clever part: if you connect a single printer to the switch, then every computer on that network can use that one printer. The switch is like a busy meeting point where all the wired devices come together to talk. On its own, though, a switch cannot reach the internet — it only connects devices that are on the same network.

The router — the doorway to the internet

A router does something different. It lets different networks talk to each other. Its most common job is to connect a small network — like your home or school — to the huge network we call the internet.

For example, a router connects Ehel Academy's network to the internet. Because of the router, any device on the school network can reach the internet — so a student can open a website, watch a lesson video, or send a message to a cousin far away. If you remember only one thing, remember this: it is the router — and only the router — that lets devices on your network reach other networks and the internet.

Connecting without wires: the wireless access point

A wired switch and a wireless access point do a similar job — they both let computers join a network. The big difference is that the wireless access point needs no cables. Devices connect to it through the air. This is perfect for devices that move around, such as:

The most common wireless access point is a Wi-Fi access point. It sends and receives signals — special invisible waves that carry data through the air to and from nearby devices. A huge advantage is that hundreds of devices can connect to a single Wi-Fi access point without any wires at all. Compare that to a wired switch, which needs one separate cable for every single device!

Wi-Fi signals only travel a short distance, though. The further you walk away from the access point, the weaker the signal becomes — until, eventually, your device drops off the network. That is why Wi-Fi access points are often fixed high up on walls or ceilings, sometimes with an aerial sticking out. An aerial is the part that helps send and receive the signals.

How is a wireless access point different from a switch?

If you put a switch and a Wi-Fi access point side by side, the biggest difference is simple: the switch uses cables, while the wireless access point uses signals through the air. A switch is best for devices that stay still, like a desktop computer or a printer. A wireless access point is best for devices you carry around, like a phone or a tablet. Both connect devices to the same network — they just do it in different ways.

Here is how the three devices fit together in a typical network. Read the diagram below from top to bottom — the internet is at the top, and the devices are at the bottom:

A simple network: the router reaches the internet; the switch connects wired devices; the wireless access point connects devices with no wires.

+-----------+ +--------------------+

+-----------+ +--------------------+

In many homes there is just ONE box that plugs into the wall — people call it 'the Wi-Fi' or 'the router'. But that single box is actually doing three jobs at once! Inside it there is a router, a switch, AND a wireless access point, all built together. In a big school or office, these three are often separate machines so they can handle many more devices.

"Give me a device — like a printer, a phone or a smart TV — and ask me whether it would connect to the network through the switch, the wireless access point, or the router. Then tell me if I was right and explain why."

This turns your tutor into a quiz partner and helps the three devices stick in your memory.

For example: "A switch connects my computer to the internet." Not quite! A switch only connects devices to each other on the SAME network. To reach the internet, the data must go through the ROUTER. The switch is the meeting point inside your network; the router is the doorway out to the wider world.

workedExamples.title: Worked example 2: How Data Travels Through Networks
workedExamples.prompt: Which device lets phones and tablets join a network with no wires? A) An Ethernet cable B) A switch C) A wireless access point D) A web server
workedExamples.solution:
You now know the hardware that joins devices together. But how does a message actually travel from your device, across the world, and arrive at exactly the right computer? That is the amazing journey you will follow in this part.

Cellular networks: the internet almost anywhere

A cellular network is another kind of wireless network, but it works over very large areas. Instead of a small Wi-Fi box on a wall, cellular networks use tall towers (you may have seen them standing high above towns and along roads). These towers send out strong signals that a smartphone can pick up from many kilometres away.

A single cell tower can reach a phone up to about 50 kilometres away, although most of the time the useful range is around 5 kilometres. Making the towers tall is important, because it means the signal is less likely to be blocked by hills or buildings. This is why a mobile phone can connect almost anywhere — from the top of a mountain to the middle of a busy city. Some cars even use cellular networks, so they can download new software or let people make calls from inside the car.

Cellular networks have one big advantage: they cover enormous areas. But they share the same weakness as Wi-Fi — they can suffer from interference. Interference is anything that gets in the way of the signal, such as thick walls or bad weather. When there is interference, the signal may not reach your device properly. This can stop your phone from connecting, or make everything very slow.

For example: Fifty kilometres is a very long way. If you ran around a 400-metre running track, you would have to go around it about 125 times to run 50 km! That is roughly the furthest a single cell tower can send its signal.

workedExamples.title: Worked example 3: Comparing the three ways to connect
workedExamples.prompt: What is the main job of a switch? A) To reach the internet B) To join wired devices on one network C) To store websites D) To send mobile signals
workedExamples.solution:
You have now met three ways for a device to connect: Wi-Fi, a wired Ethernet cable, and a cellular network (mobile data). Each one suits a different job. You would not want your phone tied to a wire while you walked around a city — and you would not use a slow, faraway cell tower to connect a printer that sits right next to your computer.

One way we compare connections is by their range — how far they reach. Another is their speed. Connection speed is measured in megabits per second, written Mbps. This is the fastest rate at which data can be sent. A higher number means data arrives more quickly, which matters a lot when you are streaming a video or downloading a big file.

IP addresses: every device has its own address

Think of the millions and millions of devices connected to the internet. When your device sends data, how does the internet know which of all those devices to deliver it to? The answer is that every device has its own unique address, called an IP address. IP stands for Internet Protocol.

An IP address is a set of numbers. A common type is made of four numbers separated by full stops, and each number is between 0 and 255. For example, a device might have the address 43.66.141.66. These numbers tell a computer exactly where to send data to, or where to fetch data from. IP addresses are usually created automatically by a small program, so you never have to type them yourself.

The best way to picture an IP address is to think of the address on a letter, or a post code. Every home has its own address so the postal worker knows exactly where to deliver each letter. In the same way, every device has its own IP address so the internet knows exactly where to deliver each piece of data. And just as no two homes on a street can share the same house number, no two devices on a network can share the same IP address — the automatic program makes sure each one is unique, so there is never any confusion.

There are two types of IP address. The older type is called IPv4 — and the world is starting to run OUT of IPv4 addresses, because there are so many devices! So a newer type was invented, called IPv6, which has an almost unlimited number of addresses — enough for every device for a very, very long time.

Here is one of the most surprising ideas about the internet. When you send a message or a photo, it does not travel as one big lump. Instead, before it is sent, the data is chopped up into many small chunks called packets. Packets are usually all about the same size.

Imagine Nadia in Hargeisa wants to send a message to Sami in Mogadishu. Her computer splits the message into, say, three packets. But each packet is not just a piece of the message — it also carries some extra labels. Every packet includes:

the IP address it was sent from (Nadia's device),

the IP address it is going to (Sami's device),

a packet number, so the pieces can be put back in the right order,

and, of course, a small piece of the actual message (the packet data).

Here is what one packet looks like inside. Notice the address labels at the top and the piece of data at the bottom:

One data packet. The 'sent from' and 'sent to' IP addresses are like the return address and destination address on an envelope.

+------------------------------------------+

+------------------------------------------+

For example: Why bother with the return address? Because if a packet gets lost on the way, the computer that was waiting for it knows exactly which device to ask to send it again. The labels make the whole system reliable.

workedExamples.title: Worked example 4: How packets travel and are put back together
workedExamples.prompt: A cellular network sends its signals using: A) Ethernet cables B) Tall towers C) Printers D) Web servers

When Nadia's packets set off across the internet, something interesting happens: they may take different routes to reach Sami. Just like cars driving from one city to another can take different roads, packets can travel by different paths. Some routes are quicker than others, so the packets often arrive in the wrong order!

This is not a problem, thanks to the packet number. When the packets arrive at their destination, Sami's computer reads the numbers and uses them to put the packets back into the correct order — like sorting shuffled pages of a story back to 1, 2, 3. Only once all the packets have arrived and are in order can the computer read the full message. Here is the whole journey in four steps:

The receiver computer notices a packet is missing, and sends a message back to the sender asking: "Please send packet 2 again, it got lost."

The sender computer sends another copy of just that one lost packet.

When the copy arrives, the receiver now has all the packets, so it puts them in order.

esafety.text: When you visit websites, only use ones that you trust and know are safe. If you are not sure about a website, always check with your teacher, your parents, or a trusted adult BEFORE you visit it. Never type your name, address, school or password into a website you do not know.

rules.title: ! — Switch, router, access point
rules.text: Switch = joins WIRED devices on one network. Router = the DOORWAY to the internet. Wireless access point = joins devices with NO wires. If you remember these three, you understand network hardware.

rules.title: ! — Only the router reaches the internet
rules.text: A switch and a wireless access point connect devices on your own network. To reach other networks and the internet, the data must go through the router.

rules.title: ! — Packets in one line
rules.text: Big data is split into small packets. Each packet has a sender IP, a destination IP, and a packet number. Packets take different routes, then are put back in order at the other end. A lost packet is simply re-sent.

rules.title: ! — Numbers for computers, names for people
rules.text: Computers find each other using IP addresses (numbers) because they only understand numbers. Humans use URLs (names) because names are far easier to remember.

rules.title: ! — The internet does not break
rules.text: When something goes wrong, it is the CONNECTIONS between computers that break, not the whole internet. Data takes another route. Companies keep backups so important services keep working.
